newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss say Portugal was second-biggest Nazi gold buyer.
newsitem.headline: Swiss say Portugal was second-biggest Nazi gold buyer.

text.p: Portugal was the second biggest buyer of Nazi German gold after Switzerland during World War Two, according to Swiss records released on Thursday of wartime gold movements through central bank accounts in Berne.

The Swiss National Bank (SNB) published a detailed list of wartime gold flows that showed Sweden, Romania, Slovakia and Spain also bought gold from Hitler's Germany through special accounts held by European central banks with the SNB.

SNB vice-president Jean-Pierre Roth said a review of the bank's own wartime records confirmed it had never hidden the amount of Nazi gold it bought or never melted down German bullion to disguise its origin.
"Besides the SNB, Portugal was the most important buyer of German gold," Roth told a news conference.

The SNB has already acknowledged it bought 1.2 billion Swiss francs worth of gold at 1940s prices from Hitler's Reichsbank and said it was hard to understand why wartime directors did not suspect the metal was looted by German troops and camp guards.

But Roth's report provided the first complete set of details of which other European central banks bought gold from Berlin through gold storage accounts run by the SNB in Berne to ease the transfer of the heavy metal from one owner to another.
According to the SNB, Portugal's central bank bought 214.6 million Swiss francs of gold in 1940s values from the Reichsbank through their Berne accounts.
"We do not know what happened outside Switzerland. Our records are only for what happened here," Roth added.
The SNB did not provide tonnages for the gold. The figures were in wartime Swiss francs, when the currency stood at about four francs to one U.S. dollar.
The official Swiss gold value during most of the war was about 4,900 Swiss francs per kilogram, the SNB said.
Other central banks that bought gold from the Reichsbank's Berne depot were Sweden (88.2 million Swiss francs), Romania (51.1 million), Slovakia (23.6 million) and Spain (7.1 million).
Another 59.1 million went to the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), a central bank for central banks based in the Swiss city of Basle.

Roth said these amounts were in addition to gold that Switzerland sold to other countries, including the Allies, the Axis powers and neutral countries. The SNB traded gold with other central banks under a policy of keeping the Swiss franc stable with gold backing.
